what: Jensen’s inequality correction for event gaps
title: gsDesignNB — Comprehensive AI Skill
text: protocol defines minimum gap \gamma counted events, naive effective rate \lambda_{\text{eff}} = \lambda / (1 + \lambda\gamma) biased upward due Jensen’s inequality applied gamma-distributed subject-level rates. second-order correction : \lambda_{\text{eff}} \approx \frac{\lambda}{1 + \lambda\gamma} \left(1 - \frac{k\lambda\gamma}{(1 + \lambda\gamma)^2}\right) matters: k \geq 0.5 gap \geq 20 days. 64-scenario simulation sweep showed naive formula underpowers 1–2.5 pp regimes; correction reduces effective-rate approximation error ~8% ~1%. negligible: k \leq 0.1 gap \leq 10 days. gap rule flows sample_size_nbinom(), nb_sim(), cut_data_by_date() planning, simulation, interim cutting consistent.

code: # Define design parameters alpha <- 0.025 k <- 2 sfu <- sfLDOF # Lan-DeMets O'Brien-Fleming approximation  # Calculate bounds for each simulation based on observed information fraction # Note: In practice, bounds are often fixed or recalculated. Here we check rejection rates. # We'll use the mean information fraction to set a single boundary for simplicity in this summary, # or we could check each trial individually. Let's check individually.  reject <- logical(n_sims) for (i in 1:n_sims) {   # Compute boundary for interim   # We need to spend alpha based on info_frac[i]   # Using gsDesign to get the boundary   # We want to spend alpha(t) = alpha * sf(t)   # But standard group sequential design defines boundaries.    # Let's use a simple error spending approach:   # Spend alpha_1 at interim based on info_frac[i]   # Spend remaining alpha at final (total alpha = 0.025)    # Interim spending   spend_interim <- sfu(alpha, t = results$info_frac[i])$spend   # Interim bound (Z-scale)   # P(Z > b1) = spend_interim   b1 <- qnorm(1 - spend_interim)    # Check interim rejection   if (results$interim_z[i] > b1) {     reject[i] <- TRUE   } else {     # Final analysis     # We need to find b2 such that P(Z1 < b1, Z2 > b2) = alpha - spend_interim     # This requires integration over the joint distribution.     # For simplicity in this vignette, we can use the asymptotic correlation     # Cor(Z1, Z2) = sqrt(info_frac)      # Using gsDesign to compute the exact boundary given the fraction     # We create a design with this fraction     gs_des <- gsDesign(k = 2, test.type = 1, alpha = alpha, sfu = sfu, timing = results$info_frac[i])     b2 <- gs_des$upper$bound[2]      if (results$final_z[i] > b2) {       reject[i] <- TRUE     }   } }  message("Power (Empirical Rejection Rate): ", mean(reject)) #> Power (Empirical Rejection Rate): 0

title: Sample size calculation for negative binomial outcomes
text: follow-times vary across subjects, using \bar{t} alone variance formula underestimates true variance. negative binomial variance depends non-linearly exposure k\mu^2 = k\lambda^2 t^2 term. Zhu Lakkis (2014) derive correction factor: Q_g = \frac{\mathrm{E}[t_g^2]}{(\mathrm{E}[t_g])^2} \ge 1 Jensen’s inequality. effective dispersion used sample size formula k_{g,\text{adj}} = k_g \cdot Q_g. exposure constant (t_i = \bar{t} ), Q = 1 adjustment needed. Variable follow-inflates Q 1, increasing required sample size. Computing \mathrm{E}[t^2]: second moment computed analogously \mathrm{E}[t] integrating m_2(u) = \mathrm{E}[\min(u, \text{dropout time})^2] enrollment distribution. Without dropout, m_2(u) = u^2. dropout rate \delta: m_2(u) = \frac{2}{\delta^2}\left(1 - e^{-\delta u}(1 + \delta u)\right) average m_2(u) across enrollment segments (appropriate handling max_followup truncation) gives \mathrm{E}[t^2_g].

text: recurrent event trials, mandatory “dead time” gap duration g event, new events can occur (e.g., recovery period). reduces effective time risk. title: Sample size calculation for negative binomial outcomes
text: single subject group g exposure t_i expected count \mu_i = \lambda_g t_i, contribution Fisher information (negative binomial log-likelihood log link): \mathcal{}_i = \frac{\mu_i}{1 + k\,\mu_i} formula intuitive limits: k = 0 (Poisson): \mathcal{}_i = \mu_i = \lambda t_i (information proportional expected events). k\mu_i \gg 1 (large overdispersion): \mathcal{}_i \approx 1/k (information saturates regardless exposure).

title: Sample size calculation for negative binomial outcomes
text: total statistical information log rate ratio : \mathcal{} = \frac{1}{\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta)} = \frac{1}{1/W_1 + 1/W_2} W_g = \sum_{\\text{group } g} \mathcal{}_i total information contributed group g. subjects group average exposure \bar{t}_g: W_g = n_g \cdot \frac{\mu_g}{1 + k_g \mu_g} = \frac{n_g}{1/\mu_g + k_g} thus: \mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta) = \frac{1/\mu_1 + k_1}{n_1} + \frac{1/\mu_2 + k_2}{n_2} exactly variance used sample size formula.

code: # Count events per subject counts_nb <- as.data.table(sim_nb)[, .(events = sum(event)), by = id]  m <- mean(counts_nb$events) v <- var(counts_nb$events) k_mom <- (v - m) / (m^2)  # Theoretical values mu_true <- 10 k_true <- 2 v_true <- mu_true + k_true * mu_true^2  # Also estimate using GLM # We use MASS::glm.nb to fit the negative binomial model # We suppress warnings because fitting intercept-only models on simulated data # can occasionally produce convergence warnings despite valid estimates. k_glm <- tryCatch(   {     fit <- suppressWarnings(MASS::glm.nb(events ~ 1, data = counts_nb))     1 / fit$theta   },   error = function(e) NA )  print(paste("True Mean:", mu_true, "| Observed Mean:", signif(m, 4))) #> [1] "True Mean: 10 | Observed Mean: 9.968" print(paste("True Variance:", v_true, "| Observed Variance:", signif(v, 4))) #> [1] "True Variance: 210 | Observed Variance: 212.9" print(paste("True Dispersion:", k_true)) #> [1] "True Dispersion: 2" print(paste("Estimated Dispersion (MoM):", signif(k_mom, 4))) #> [1] "Estimated Dispersion (MoM): 2.042" print(paste("Estimated Dispersion (GLM):", signif(k_glm, 4))) #> [1] "Estimated Dispersion (GLM): 2.018"

# Information fraction at final analysis # If final_info < target_info, fraction < 1.  # However, for the final analysis, we typically want to spend all remaining alpha. # We can treat the current info as the "maximum" info for the spending function.  # Example group sequential design (O'Brien-Fleming spending) # We assume the interim was at the observed information fraction info_fractions <- c(ssr_res$info_fraction, final_info / ssr_res$target_info)  # If final fraction < 1, we can force it to 1 to spend all alpha,  # effectively accepting the lower power. # Or we can use the actual information fractions in a spending function approach.  # Let's assume we want to spend all alpha at the final analysis regardless of info. # We set the final timing to 1. info_fractions_spending <- c(ssr_res$info_fraction, 1)  # Update bounds gs_update <- gsDesign(   k = 2,   test.type = 1,   alpha = alpha_plan,   sfu = sfLDOF,   usTime = info_fractions_spending,   n.I = c(ssr_res$unblinded_info, final_info) )  gsBoundSummary(gs_update,     deltaname = "RR",     logdelta = TRUE,     Nname = "Information",     timename = "Month",     digits = 4,     ddigits = 2) |> gt() |>   tab_header(     title = "Updated Group Sequential Design Bounds",     subtitle = paste0(       "Final Information = ", round(final_info, 2)     )   ) # Test statistic z_score <- coef(fit_final)["treatmentExperimental"] / sqrt(var_beta) # Note: gsDesign assumes Z > 0 for efficacy.  # Our model gives log(RR) < 0 for efficacy. # So Z_stat = - (log(RR)) / SE z_stat <- -coef(fit_final)["treatmentExperimental"] / sqrt(var_beta)  cat("Z-statistic:", z_stat, "
") #> Z-statistic: 1.24208 cat("Final Bound:", gs_update$upper$bound[2], "
") #> Final Bound: 1.959964  if (z_stat > gs_update$upper$bound[2]) {   cat("Reject Null Hypothesis

title: Method of Moments Estimation for Negative Binomial Parameters — estimate_nb_mom
text: method moments estimator dispersion parameter \(k\) derived equating theoretical variance observed second central moment, accounting varying exposure times. given group rate \(\lambda\), expected count subject \(\) \(\mu_i = \lambda t_i\). variance \(V_i = \mu_i + k \mu_i^2\). estimator calculated : $$\hat{k} = \max\left(0, \frac{\sum (y_i - \hat{\mu}_i)^2 - \sum y_i}{\sum \hat{\mu}_i^2}\right)$$ \(y_i\) number events, \(t_i\) exposure time, \(\hat{\mu}_i = \hat{\lambda} t_i\) estimated expected count. multiple groups present, numerator denominator summed across groups estimate common \(k\).

title: Simulate recurrent events with fixed follow-up — nb_sim
text: simulation generates data consistent negative binomial models described Friede Schmidli (2010) Mütze et al. (2019). Specifically, simulates Gamma-distributed frailty variable individual (dispersion > 0), acts multiplier individual's event rate. Events generated according Poisson process subject-specific rate. explicitly, subject baseline rate \(\lambda\) exposure time \(t\), model used Gamma–Poisson mixture: $$\Lambda_i \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\text{shape}=1/k,\ \text{scale}=k\lambda), \quad Y_i \mid \Lambda_i \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\Lambda_i t).$$ Marginally, \(Y_i\) follows negative binomial distribution \(\mathrm{E}[Y_i]=\mu=\lambda t\) \(\mathrm{Var}(Y_i)=\mu + k\mu^2\). \(k\) package dispersion parameter (corresponds \(1/\theta\) MASS::glm.nb() terminology).

title: Sample size calculation for negative binomial outcomes — sample_size_nbinom
text: lambda1 Event rate group 1 (control), events per unit time. lambda2 Event rate group 2 (treatment), events per unit time. dispersion Dispersion parameter \(k\) \(\mathrm{Var}(Y) = \mu + k\mu^2\). Equivalent 1/size stats::rnbinom(). Can scalar (common dispersion) vector length 2 (group-specific: control, treatment). power Target power (\(1 - \beta\)). NULL, power computed given accrual rates (sample size scaling). Default 0.9. alpha Significance level. Default 0.025. sided Number sides test: 1 (one-sided) 2 (two-sided). Default 1. ratio Allocation ratio \(r = n_2/n_1\). Default 1 (equal allocation). rr0 Rate ratio null hypothesis (\(\lambda_2 / \lambda_1\)). Default 1 (superiority). non-inferiority, use value > 1 (e.g., 1.1). super-superiority, use value < 1 (e.g., 0.8). accrual_rate Vector accrual rates (patients per unit time) recruitment segment. accrual_duration Vector durations accrual segment. Must length accrual_rate. trial_duration Total planned duration trial. trial_duration less sum accrual_duration, accrual truncated trial_duration. dropout_rate Dropout hazard rate. Default 0. Can vector length 2 group-specific dropout (control, treatment). max_followup Maximum follow-time patient. Default NULL (infinite). Can vector length 2 group-specific caps. event_gap Gap duration event new events counted (e.g., recovery period). Default NULL (gap). specified, effective rate reduced \(\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}} = \lambda / (1 + \lambda \cdot \mathrm{gap})\).

title: Sample size calculation for negative binomial outcomes — sample_size_nbinom
text: object class sample_size_nbinom_result, list containing: inputs Named list original function arguments. n1 Sample size group 1 (control). n2 Sample size group 2 (treatment). n_total Total sample size (\(n_1 + n_2\)). alpha Significance level used. sided One-sided two-sided test. power Power test. exposure Average calendar exposure \(\bar{t}_g\) (vector length 2 control treatment). exposure_at_risk_n1 Average -risk exposure group 1 (adjusted event gap). exposure_at_risk_n2 Average -risk exposure group 2 (adjusted event gap). events_n1 Expected number events group 1. events_n2 Expected number events group 2. total_events Total expected number events. variance Variance log rate ratio \(\mathrm{Var}(\hat\theta)\). accrual_rate Accrual rate(s) used (possibly scaled achieve target power). accrual_duration Accrual duration(s) used.

title: Sample size calculation for negative binomial outcomes — sample_size_nbinom
text: sample size group 1 : $$n_1 = \frac{(z_{\alpha/s} + z_\beta)^2 \tilde{V}}{(\theta - \theta_0)^2}$$ \(\theta = \log(\lambda_2/\lambda_1)\), \(\theta_0 = \log(\mathrm{rr}_0)\), : $$\tilde{V} = \left(\frac{1}{\mu_1} + k_1\right) + \frac{1}{r}\left(\frac{1}{\mu_2} + k_2\right)$$ \(\mu_g = \lambda_g \bar{t}_g\) expected event count \(\bar{t}_g\) average exposure group \(g\).

title: Sample size calculation for negative binomial outcomes — sample_size_nbinom
text: average exposure \(\bar{t}_g\) accounts piecewise accrual, exponential dropout, maximum follow-truncation. dropout rate \(\delta > 0\), expected exposure patient potential follow-\(u\) \(m(u) = (1 - e^{-\delta u})/\delta\). overall average weighted mean across accrual segments.

title: Sample size calculation for negative binomial outcomes — sample_size_nbinom
text: follow-times variable, dispersion inflated factor \(Q_g = \mathrm{E}[t_g^2] / (\mathrm{E}[t_g])^2 \ge 1\) (Zhu & Lakkis, 2014) account non-linear dependence NB variance exposure.

title: Sample size calculation for negative binomial outcomes — sample_size_nbinom
text: event_gap > 0, naive effective rate \(\lambda / (1 + \lambda g)\) overestimates true population-level effective rate subject-level heterogeneity (frailty). Gamma-Poisson mixture, subject's rate \(\Lambda_i \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(1/k, k\lambda)\) random. Since \(f(x) = x/(1+xg)\) concave, Jensen's inequality gives \(\mathrm{E}[f(\Lambda)] < f(\mathrm{E}[\Lambda])\). second-order Taylor correction applied: $$\lambda_{\mathrm{eff}} \approx \frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda g}   \left(1 - \frac{k \lambda g}{(1+\lambda g)^2}\right)$$ uses \(f''(\lambda) = -2g/(1+\lambda g)^3\) \(\mathrm{Var}(\Lambda) = k\lambda^2\).

what: Robust NB fallback: method-of-moments replaces Poisson under genuine overdispersion
title: gsDesignNB 0.3.1 (development)
text: mutze_test(), calculate_blinded_info(), unblinded_ssr() now fall back method--moments (MoM) estimation via estimate_nb_mom() maximum likelihood negative binomial fit converge returns extreme-overdispersion shape estimate. Previously, Poisson fallback used “near-Poisson” “extreme-overdispersion” regimes; latter anti-conservative Poisson variance underestimates true NB variance genuine overdispersion. MoM fallback computes Wald standard error observed Fisher information formula \mathcal{} = 1/(1/W_1 + 1/W_2) W_g = \sum_i \mu_{g,}/(1 + \hat{k}\mu_{g,}), preserving NB variance structure without requiring ML convergence. mutze_test() gains mom_threshold argument (default 20, corresponding \hat{k} > 20) controls MoM branch triggered. existing poisson_threshold default reduced 1000 50 (\hat{k} < 0.02) since NB Poisson Wald standard errors numerically indistinguishable point. three functions now return additional fallback element output ("ml", "mom", "poisson") downstream simulation engines can record estimator used interim.

what: Jensen’s inequality correction for event gaps
title: gsDesignNB 0.3.0
text: Applied second-order Taylor correction effective rate formula dispersion (k > 0) event gap (g > 0) present. naive formula \lambda/(1+\lambda g) overestimates population-level effective rate due Jensen’s inequality (subject-level frailty makes f(x)=x/(1+xg) concave). corrected formula \lambda_{\text{eff}} \approx \frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda g}(1 - k\lambda g/(1+\lambda g)^2). Correction applied sample_size_nbinom() compute_info_at_time(). Simulation study across multiple scenarios (10,000 replicates ) confirms corrected design maintains nominal conservative power, naive formula increasingly underpowers k g grow.
